134.title: Asking for someone absent
134.hook: an angel says, and for you the same, when you pray for someone behind their back (Muslim)
134.howItsDone: Many Muslims make du'a for family, friends and fellow believers by name in their private prayers, without telling them, following the hadith that an angel says 'and for you the same'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: good in this world and the next, the short du'a from Surah al-Baqarah. Your line was good here, good there. Did you ask for both? Day one hundred thirty-four.
screen: `GOOD IN THIS WORLD AND THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: Everybody knows what it's like to be talked about behind their back. Usually it isn't good. A comment in a group chat you weren't supposed to see. A silence when you walk into the room. Now flip it. Imagine finding out, years later, that someone you barely thought about had been mentioning your name, quietly, for a long time, asking for good things for you. You never knew. They never told you. There's a hadith about exactly that, and it adds a twist. Someone else is listening. Today: asking for someone absent.
screen: `TALKED ABOUT BEHIND YOUR BACK.` → `NOW FLIP IT.` → `SOMEONE ELSE IS LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Sahih Muslim reports it from Abu al-Darda', one of the companions. The Prophet ﷺ said: whenever a Muslim makes du'a for his brother in his absence, behind his back, an angel says: ameen, and for you the same. In Arabic, wa laka bi-mithl. And for you, its like. So the moment you ask for good for someone who can't hear you, the same good is asked for you. Not by you. By an angel. Another version in Muslim adds that an angel is appointed at the person's head for just this purpose. Why does the absence matter? Because it's the purest kind of asking. There's no credit in it. The other person will never thank you. You can't be doing it to look kind. A report in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi goes further, saying the du'a answered most quickly is the one made by someone absent for someone absent. The Qur'an itself is full of people asking for others. Ibrahim asks for forgiveness for himself, his parents and the believers. Surah al-Hashr describes later believers asking forgiveness for those who came before them in faith, people they never met. It's a web of names, most of them never spoken aloud. Notice, too, what the hadith doesn't say. It doesn't tell you to pray for others so you'll get something. The good comes back as a side effect, almost a surprise. You go out of your way for someone else, and you find you've been included. It's a quiet economy of the heart where giving never leaves you short.
screen: `AN ANGEL SAYS: AND FOR YOU THE SAME.` · `NO CREDIT, NO THANKS.` · `IBRAHIM ASKS FOR HIS PARENTS.` · `THE GOOD COMES BACK AS A SURPRISE.` · then, large: `WA LAKA BI-MITHL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone who'll never know. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Think of someone who has no idea you're thinking of them. A coworker who seems tired. A neighbor you only wave at. Someone you've fallen out with. Hold their face in mind. If you pray, you can ask Allah for one good thing for them, in your own words, silently. If you don't, simply wish them one good thing, as specifically as you can. Don't tell them afterward. Let it stay behind their back. The bell holds the time.
Asking for someone absent. A du'a made behind someone's back, which the hadith says an angel answers: and for you the same. Today's word.

Your line: and the same for you. Every time someone crosses your mind today, a name in your inbox, a face on the bus, wish them one good thing, silently, and leave it there. Day one hundred thirty-four.

135.title: The times that open
135.hook: in prostration, the last third of the night, between adhan and iqamah, while fasting
135.howItsDone: Many Muslims save their most important du'a for prostration, the last third of the night, the time between the adhan and the iqamah, and the moments before breaking a fast.

segments.voice: Yesterday: asking for someone absent, and the angel who answers. Your line was and the same for you. Whose name crossed your mind, and did you wish them one good thing? Day one hundred thirty-five.
screen: `ASKING FOR SOMEONE ABSENT — AND THE SAME FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Every office has one. The manager whose door is technically always open, but everyone knows the good time to ask is Friday afternoon, after lunch, when things are calm. Timing isn't everything, but it's something. This week we've said du'a can be made anywhere, any time, in any words. That's still true. The door is never locked. But the hadith collections also name certain moments when the door is described as especially wide open. Moments to save your biggest asks for. Today: the times that open.
screen: `THE DOOR IS ALWAYS OPEN.` → `BUT SOME MOMENTS ARE WIDER.` → `SAVE YOUR BIGGEST ASKS.`

segments.voice: Here are four of them. The first you already know from day one hundred five: in prostration. Sahih Muslim reports that the closest a servant is to his Lord is while prostrating, so ask much there. Forehead on the floor, and many Muslims pour their private requests into those few seconds, silently, in their own words. The second is the last third of the night. Bukhari and Muslim report that every night, when the last third remains, our Lord descends to the nearest heaven and says: who is calling on Me, that I may answer? Who is asking of Me, that I may give? Who is seeking forgiveness, that I may forgive? Scholars have long differed on how to understand that descent; many simply accept it without asking how. Either way, the picture is of the whole sky listening while almost everyone is asleep. It's why some Muslims set an alarm for an hour before dawn. The third is small and ordinary: between the adhan and the iqamah, the call to prayer and the call to stand. Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi report that a du'a made in that gap is not turned back. Those few minutes when people are waiting in the mosque, checking the time, are described as an open door. The fourth is while fasting. Tirmidhi reports that the fasting person's du'a is among those not rejected, and many Muslims make du'a just before breaking the fast at sunset. There are others: part of Friday, while traveling, when it rains. But notice what these four share. Lowered. Awake while others sleep. Waiting. Hungry. Moments when a person is a little emptier than usual.
screen: `FIRST: IN PROSTRATION.` · `THE LAST THIRD OF THE NIGHT.` · `BETWEEN THE ADHAN AND THE IQAMAH.` · `WHILE FASTING.` · then, large: `A LITTLE EMPTIER THAN USUAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one time this week. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Run through the four in your mind. Face on the floor. The quiet hour before dawn. The waiting minutes before a prayer. The last minute of an empty stomach. Which one could you actually reach this week? Choose one. Picture it: where you'll be, what the room looks like. If you pray, decide now what you'll ask for when you get there. If not, decide what you'll sit quietly with. The bell holds the time.
The times that open. Prostration, the last third of the night, the gap between the adhan and the iqamah, and the fast: moments the hadith describe as especially open to du'a. Today's word.
Your line: knock at the open door. Put the time you chose into your calendar or set an alarm for it now, and keep one question ready for when it comes. Day one hundred thirty-five.

136.title: Before sleep
136.hook: in Your name I die and I live, before lying down (Bukhari)
136.howItsDone: Many Muslims make wudu before bed, lie on the right side, recite the last three surahs and say 'bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya', and on waking praise Allah for giving life again.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the times that open, from prostration to the hour before dawn. Your line was knock at the open door. Did you choose your time? Day one hundred thirty-six.
screen: `THE TIMES THAT OPEN — KNOCK AT THE OPEN DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the last thing most of us do every day: scroll. Lights off, face lit blue, one more video, one more headline. Then the phone drops, and we're gone. Seven or eight hours when we don't know where we are, can't guard anything, can't answer anyone. It's the most helpless we'll be all day, and we treat it as nothing. This whole week has been about asking. Just ask. Open hands. He is near. Good here and there. For the absent. At the open times. It ends at the edge of sleep. Today: before sleep.
screen: `THE LAST THING: ONE MORE VIDEO.` → `THE MOST HELPLESS HOURS.` → `A WEEK OF ASKING ENDS HERE.`

segments.voice: Bukhari reports from the companion Hudhayfah that when the Prophet ﷺ lay down at night, he put his hand under his cheek and said: bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya. In Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. It's very short. And it's striking. It calls sleep a kind of dying. That isn't just poetry. The Qur'an, in Surah az-Zumar, says Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and also takes, in their sleep, the souls that have not died; He keeps the ones whose death is decreed and sends the others back until a set time. Every night, in this picture, is a small rehearsal. You let go of everything, and you're handed back in the morning. So the same hadith gives the waking words too: alhamdulillahi alladhi ahyana ba'da ma amatana wa ilayhin-nushur. Praise be to Allah, who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the rising. The first thought of the day is thanks for being handed back. Around those two lines, the tradition gathers other habits. Many Muslims make wudu before bed, lie on the right side, and recite the last three short surahs, al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas, blowing lightly into cupped hands and passing them over the body, as Bukhari reports the Prophet did. Some add the Verse of the Throne. None of it is long. It takes less time than one more video. And it changes what the last thing is. Not a headline. A name.
screen: `IN YOUR NAME I DIE AND I LIVE.` · `SLEEP AS A SMALL DYING.` · `HANDED BACK IN THE MORNING.` · `WUDU, RIGHT SIDE, THREE SURAHS.` · then, large: `THE LAST THING IS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse it now, and say it before sleeping tonight. Sit or lie back comfortably. Rest one hand under your cheek, or just let your head tip slightly to the right. Let the day go, one breath at a time: the work, the messages, the argument. If you pray, you can say it quietly: bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya, or in English, in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. If not, simply notice how much you're about to let go of, and let it go. Stay heavy and still. The bell holds the time.
Before sleep. The Prophet's words at bedtime: in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live, and on waking, praise for being given life again. Today's word.
Your line: in your name I sleep. Tonight, put the phone down one minute earlier than usual, and make the last thing you think or say a name, not a headline. Day one hundred thirty-six.

137.title: What a mosque is
137.hook: the place of prostration, open for prayer, learning and gathering
137.howItsDone: Muslims gather at the mosque for the five daily prayers and Friday prayer, and for classes, community meals, weddings and funerals; many mosques also welcome visitors.

segments.voice: Yesterday: before sleep, in Your name I die and I live. Your line was in your name I sleep. Was the last thing last night a name, or a headline? Day one hundred thirty-seven.
screen: `BEFORE SLEEP — IN YOUR NAME I SLEEP.`

segments.voice: You've probably driven past one. Maybe a grand building with a dome and a tall minaret. Maybe a converted shop on a strip mall, with a hand-painted sign and a row of shoes visible through the glass door. Maybe a room in a university basement. From the outside, they look nothing alike. And a lot of people who aren't Muslim have never been inside one, and aren't sure they'd be allowed. This week, the path walks you through a visit, one step at a time. It starts with the name on the sign. Today: what a mosque is.
screen: `A DOME, A STRIP MALL, A BASEMENT.` → `NEVER BEEN INSIDE?` → `A WEEK-LONG VISIT, STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is masjid. You met its root on day one hundred five: sujud, prostration. A masjid is simply the place of prostration, the place where people put their foreheads on the floor. The English word mosque probably came to us through the Spanish mezquita, from the same Arabic. Notice what the name doesn't require. Not a dome. Not a minaret. Not even a building. Bukhari reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that the whole earth has been made a masjid for him, a place of prayer. That's why you'll see Muslims pray in parks, airports and parking lots. Any clean ground will do. So what makes a building a mosque? Go back to the first ones. When the Prophet arrived in Medina, one of the first things he did was build one, with his own hands alongside the companions, as the reports describe: walls of mud brick, pillars of palm trunks, a roof of palm leaves. And look at what went on inside. The five prayers, of course. But also teaching. Delegations received. Poor companions with nowhere else to live sleeping on a shaded platform at the back, known as the Suffah. Bukhari even reports a tent pitched in the mosque to nurse a wounded man, and, on an Eid, men from Abyssinia putting on a display with their spears, while the Prophet's wife Aisha watched. It was a house of prayer that was also a school, a shelter, a clinic and a town square. Many mosques today try to be the same: prayer five times a day, weekend classes, food drives, weddings, funerals. And many welcome visitors who simply want to see.
screen: `MASJID — THE PLACE OF PROSTRATION.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH IS A MASJID.` · `MUD BRICK AND PALM TRUNKS.` · `SCHOOL, SHELTER, CLINIC, SQUARE.` · then, large: `A PLACE TO BOW, AND MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, in two parts. First, sit, and picture the ground you're on right now, the floor under your chair, the earth under the building. If the whole earth is a place to bow, this spot counts too. Let that settle for a few breaths. Then, when the bell has finished, open a map and look for the nearest mosque. Notice its name, how far it is, whether it's a big building or a small room. You don't have to go. Just know where it is. For now, breathe, and feel the ground. The bell holds the time.
Masjid. A mosque: the place of prostration, open for prayer, learning and gathering. Today's word.
Your line: a place to bow. As you move through today, notice one spot, a park, a quiet corner, the floor of your room, and think: this could be a place to bow. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

screen: `DAY 137 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SHOES OFF, RIGHT FOOT IN.`

138.title: Shoes off, right foot in
138.hook: shoes at the door, enter with the right foot, a greeting prayer on the lips
138.howItsDone: At the mosque, Muslims leave their shoes at the door, step in with the right foot first saying 'Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik', and leave with the left foot, asking Allah for His bounty.

segments.voice: Yesterday: masjid, the place of prostration, and a school, shelter and town square too. Your line was a place to bow. Did you find the nearest mosque on the map? Day one hundred thirty-eight.

Think about the homes where you take your shoes off at the door. Maybe your grandmother's. Maybe a friend's, with a neat rack in the hallway and a basket of slippers. You step out of the outside world, literally, and your feet land on something softer. You lower your voice a little without being told. Now picture the door of a mosque. A long shelf, or just a heap, of shoes: sneakers, loafers, tiny children's sandals, work boots. That pile is the first thing you meet. Today: shoes off, right foot in.
screen: `SHOES AT GRANDMA'S DOOR.` → `STEPPING OUT OF THE OUTSIDE.` → `A PILE OF SHOES AT THE MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Why shoes off? The simplest answer is the floor. In a mosque, people put their foreheads on that carpet five times a day. You wouldn't walk across a kitchen table in the shoes you wore through a parking lot. So the shoes stay at the door, and the carpet stays clean. It isn't that shoes are forbidden in prayer as such. Bukhari reports that the companion Anas was asked whether the Prophet ﷺ ever prayed in his sandals, and he said yes, on clean ground. But on a shared carpet, shoes off is the custom almost everywhere. Then the right foot. Aisha said, in Bukhari, that the Prophet liked to begin with the right in everything he could: putting on his sandals, combing his hair, washing for prayer. So many Muslims step into the mosque right foot first, and step out left foot first. It's a small thing. It turns an ordinary doorway into a moment you notice. And the words on the lips. Sahih Muslim reports that when you enter the mosque, you say: Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik. O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy. And when you leave: O Allah, I ask You for Your bounty. Mercy inside, provision outside. For a visitor, a few more things help. Modest, loose clothes. Many mosques ask women to cover their hair, and often keep scarves at the door. Speak softly. And don't walk directly in front of someone who's praying; wait, or go around behind them. None of it is a test. It's the same thing you do at grandma's: you come in gently.
screen: `SHOES OFF: FACES GO ON THIS FLOOR.` · `THE RIGHT FOOT FIRST.` · `OPEN FOR ME THE DOORS OF YOUR MERCY.` · `DON'T CROSS IN FRONT OF SOMEONE PRAYING.` · then, large: `COME IN GENTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enter a room slowly. Stand up, and walk to the nearest doorway. If you're wearing shoes and it's easy, slip them off. Pause at the threshold. Take one breath. Then step through with your right foot first, and let the left follow. If you pray, you can say, as you step, Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik. If not, just notice the change: the air, the floor, the sound. Then sit down in the new room, and stay still. The bell holds the time.
Shoes off. The first step into a mosque: shoes at the door, the right foot first, and a request for the doors of mercy. Today's word.
Your line: come in gently. Every time you walk into a room today, a kitchen, an office, a meeting, pause at the door for one breath before you step in. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

139.title: The washing place
139.hook: most mosques have a place for wudu near the entrance
139.howItsDone: Most mosques have a wudu area near the entrance, usually separate for men and women, where worshippers sit at low taps to wash hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head and feet before prayer; many make wudu at home first.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shoes off, right foot in, and a request for the doors of mercy. Your line was come in gently. Did you pause at a doorway? Day one hundred thirty-nine.

Walk into almost any mosque, and before you reach the prayer hall you'll hear it: running water. Follow the sound and you'll find a room that surprises a lot of first-time visitors. A long row of taps set low in the wall. A line of little stools, or a stone ledge to sit on. A drain running along the floor. People with sleeves rolled up past the elbow and trouser legs pushed up, washing their feet in a public room, perfectly calmly. It's not the bathroom. It's one of the most important rooms in the building. Today: the washing place.
screen: `FOLLOW THE SOUND OF WATER.` → `LOW TAPS, LITTLE STOOLS, A DRAIN.` → `NOT THE BATHROOM.`

segments.voice: It's where people make wudu, the washing before prayer, and most mosques have one near the entrance, often a separate one for men and for women. The order comes from Surah al-Ma'idah, chapter five, verse six. In Pickthall's translation it begins: O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, and lightly rub your heads and wash your feet up to the ankles. From the hadith come the rest: the hands first, rinsing the mouth and nose, and doing most things three times. That's why the taps are low. You sit, you wash, you lift one foot at a time to the water. A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives the washing a second meaning. When a person washes the face, every wrong the eyes looked at leaves with the water, or with its last drop. When they wash the hands, what the hands did. When they wash the feet, where the feet walked. The water is doing more than rinsing. And the walk matters too. Sahih Muslim reports that whoever purifies himself at home and then walks to one of the houses of Allah, each step erases a wrong and the next raises him a degree. So many people make wudu at home and use the washing place only to top up. There are manners here too. Bukhari reports that the Prophet ﷺ made wudu with about a double handful of water. Not a flood. So people try not to leave taps running, not to splash their neighbor, and to leave the floor as dry as they found it. Wash, and then walk in.
screen: `WUDU, NEAR THE ENTRANCE.` · `FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET.` · `WRONGS LEAVE WITH THE LAST DROP.` · `A DOUBLE HANDFUL, NOT A FLOOD.` · then, large: `WASH, THEN WALK IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make wudu slowly at home, or picture it. If you can get to a sink, go now. Turn the tap on low. Wash your hands. Your mouth and nose, if you like. Your face, from the hairline to the chin. Your arms to the elbows. A wet hand over your hair. Your feet, if you can. Slowly, using as little water as you can. If you can't move right now, do it in your mind, feeling each part. Then sit, and notice where the water was. The bell holds the time.
The washing place. The room near a mosque's entrance where people make wudu before they pray. Today's word.
Your line: wash, then enter. Before one important thing today, a meeting, a meal, a hard conversation, wash your hands and face slowly first, and walk in fresh. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

140.title: Mihrab and minbar
140.hook: the niche shows the qiblah; the steps are where the Friday sermon is given
140.howItsDone: In the mosque the imam leads the prayer standing before the mihrab, the niche marking the qiblah, and gives the Friday sermon from the minbar, a stepped pulpit beside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the washing place, the room of low taps near the door. Your line was wash, then enter. Did you walk into something fresh? Day one hundred forty.

You've washed. Shoes are off. You step into the prayer hall, and the first surprise is how empty it is. No pews. No altar. No statues. Mostly carpet, often with lines woven into it. But look at the far wall. There's a curved niche set into it, sometimes plain, sometimes covered in tiles and calligraphy. And just to its right, a small staircase that leads nowhere, with a little platform at the top. Two pieces of furniture in a nearly empty room. Each has a job. Today: mihrab and minbar.
screen: `NO PEWS, NO ALTAR, NO STATUES.` → `A CURVED NICHE IN THE WALL.` → `STAIRS THAT LEAD NOWHERE.`

segments.voice: The niche is the mihrab. Its job is simple: it marks the qiblah, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which you met on day ninety-nine. Walk into any mosque in the world, look for the mihrab, and you know which way everyone will face. The imam who leads the prayer stands in front of it, and in many mosques its curve helps carry his voice back into the room. The word itself is old. The Qur'an uses it in the story of Maryam, the mother of Isa: whenever Zakariyya came to her in the mihrab, her place of prayer, he found food with her, and asked where it came from. In the Prophet's own mosque there was no niche at all; historians say the curved mihrab came a few generations later, when that mosque was rebuilt. The staircase is the minbar, the pulpit, where the imam gives the sermon at the Friday prayer. And its story is one of the most tender in Bukhari. At first, the Prophet ﷺ gave his sermons leaning against the trunk of a palm tree. Then a minbar of three wooden steps was made for him. The first Friday he climbed it, the companions heard the old palm trunk cry out, like a child, or like a camel longing for its young. The Prophet came down, and put his hand on it, and held it until it went quiet. The mihrab says where to face. The minbar says who will speak. But neither is holy in itself. What they do together is point a whole room one way, so that the rich man and the cleaner, the old and the new, face the same way.
screen: `MIHRAB — THE NICHE THAT SHOWS THE QIBLAH.` · `MARYAM IN THE MIHRAB.` · `MINBAR — THE STEPS FOR THE SERMON.` · `THE PALM TRUNK THAT CRIED.` · then, large: `EVERYONE FACES THE SAME WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where a room points. Look around the room you're in. Every room faces somewhere: toward a screen, a window, a desk, a door. Where do the chairs point? Where does your body turn by default? Now, if you know it, turn to face the direction of Mecca, or just toward a window, somewhere with light. Sit, and let your whole body face one way. If other people are near, notice that you could all be facing the same way without saying a word. The bell holds the time.
Mihrab. The niche in a mosque's front wall that shows the qiblah, the direction everyone faces in prayer. Today's word.

Your line: everyone faces the same way. Once today, in a line, a meeting or a crowd, notice that you're all facing the same way, and let that make you a little kinder to the person beside you. Day one hundred forty.
